title: SC Justice Bhuyan Slams Collegium's Return to Opacity in Judicial Appointments
excerpt: Speaking at the launch of a judicial transparency report, Justice Ujjal Bhuyan said the Collegium's failure to give reasons for appointments allows unsuitable candidates into the judiciary and is a disservice to deserving judges.
body:
• Supreme Court Justice Ujjal Bhuyan criticised the Collegium for abandoning the practice of giving reasons for judicial appointments, calling it a disservice to deserving judges
  • Justice Bhuyan flagged that the last three Collegium resolutions contain no reasons for recommending elevations, reversing earlier practice
  • Senior Advocate Saurabh Kirpal drew parallels with the US Senate confirmation process, arguing that Indian judicial appointments lack comparable public scrutiny

Supreme Court Justice Ujjal Bhuyan has mounted a sharp critique of the Collegium system's growing opacity, warning that the body's failure to disclose reasons for judicial appointments risks allowing unsuitable candidates into the higher judiciary.

"By not giving reasons, you are actually doing a disservice to judges who have done tremendous work," Justice Bhuyan said at the launch of the Judicial Transparency Index, a report by the Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy's JALDI initiative that assesses disclosure practices across the Supreme Court and High Courts.

"By not doing this, we are allowing some kind of people who come inside the judiciary who will later go on to describe a group of people as 'ants' this and that. It's completely unconstitutional. To prevent entry of such people, there should be some discussion; there should be some reasons given."

— Justice Ujjal Bhuyan, Supreme Court of India

The reference was to a former High Court judge who had sparked controversy with remarks allegedly targeting a community — an episode Justice Bhuyan held up as evidence of what unchecked appointments can produce.

A Measurable Retreat From Transparency

Justice Bhuyan pointed to a concrete and verifiable shift. The last three Supreme Court Collegium resolutions, including the most recent one in 2025, contain no reasons whatsoever for recommending judicial elevations. Earlier resolutions, by contrast, provided at least some justification for each recommendation.

"They may not have been exhaustive. Some may even say they were somewhat formulaic or copy-paste in nature. But at least some reasons were given to justify the recommendations," Justice Bhuyan observed, before asking: "Is this a step back from the principle of transparency?"

He described this gap as a "reflexive gap" — a judiciary that has embraced openness in its adjudicative function but remains conspicuously guarded about its own appointment processes. "Deliberations over the elevation and transfer of judges remain confidential; reasons for rejecting or deferring a recommendation are rarely disclosed in full; and the criteria applied are not codified in any publicly accessible instrument," he said.

The US Comparison and the Kirpal Case

Senior Advocate Saurabh Kirpal, who joined Justice Bhuyan on the panel, drew a pointed comparison with the United States. American Supreme Court justices may be ideological, Kirpal acknowledged, but they undergo intense public scrutiny through Senate confirmation hearings.

"Every question, every aspect of their life is laid bare, split up threadbare. The one thing you cannot say is they have evaded scrutiny," Kirpal said, arguing that disclosing reasons ensures there is no arbitrariness or capriciousness.

Justice Bhuyan cited the Collegium's own resolution of January 18, 2023, reiterating the recommendation for Kirpal's appointment as a Delhi High Court judge, as an example of well-reasoned deliberation. "The reasons given by the Supreme Court are quite convincing," he said — before noting that three and a half years had passed with no action on the recommendation.

What's Next

Justice Bhuyan recommended that the JALDI team investigate the opacity of the Collegium system as part of its transparency work. He stressed that citizens have a fundamental right to know who their judges are and what judgments they have delivered.

"Citizens have a right to know what is happening in the courts. They have a right to know who their judges are. All this should be in the public domain," he said.

The remarks carry weight coming from a sitting Supreme Court judge who has previously criticised executive interference in the Collegium process. In a lecture at ILS Law College, Pune earlier this year, Justice Bhuyan had warned against transfers of judges at the government's request, calling it a "striking intrusion" that compromised the system's integrity.

His latest intervention shifts the spotlight from external pressure to internal accountability — suggesting that the Collegium must reform itself if it wishes to retain legitimacy as the sole gatekeeper of judicial appointments in India.
